lead: A resistor load wastes the gain of a differential pair: more gain needs a bigger resistor, and a bigger resistor drops more DC voltage and eats the output swing. Replace the resistors with a PMOS current mirror and the load becomes a high small-signal resistance that drops almost no DC voltage. The mirror also folds the two side currents into one node, so a differential input becomes a single-ended output. Every CMOS op-amp input stage is built this way.
prereq: You need 5.1 for the differential pair, 5.3 for the mirror, and the MOSFET output resistance ro = 1/(λID) from Unit 2, Small-signal models.

sections.h3: Why the load resistor limits gain

blocks.text: A differential pair with two drain resistors turns the input difference into a difference of drain currents, and the resistors turn that current back into a voltage. Taken at one drain only, the gain is small.

blocks.where: A<sub>d</sub> is the single-ended voltage gain in V/V; g<sub>m1</sub> is the transconductance of one input transistor in siemens (A/V); R<sub>D</sub> is the drain resistor in ohms. The ½ appears because an input difference v<sub>id</sub> moves each drain current by only g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>id</sub>/2.

blocks.text: The resistor costs you twice. A large R<sub>D</sub> carries the bias current I<sub>D</sub> and drops I<sub>D</sub>R<sub>D</sub> volts, so the output node sits near a supply rail and the swing left for the signal is small. On-chip resistors are also inaccurate, often ±20 %, so the gain is inaccurate too. A current-source load changes both facts: the DC voltage across it is only a few hundred millivolts, while its small-signal resistance r<sub>o</sub> is tens to hundreds of kilohms. Gain then follows g<sub>m</sub>r<sub>o</sub>, not g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>D</sub>.

The standard CMOS input stage uses five transistors. M1 and M2 are the NMOS input pair, M5 is the NMOS tail current source, and M3 and M4 form a PMOS current mirror that acts as the load. Some syllabi call the block an active-loaded differential amplifier; others call it a CMOS OTA core. Both names mean the same five-transistor circuit.

items: M5 sinks a fixed tail current I<sub>tail</sub>; matched inputs share it equally, so each side carries I<sub>tail</sub>/2.
Apply v<sub>id</sub>. M1's drain current rises by g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>id</sub>/2 and M2's falls by the same amount (signs swap if you invert the input).
M3 is diode-connected, so it absorbs M1's current and sets the gate voltage of M4.
M4 shares that gate, so it copies M1's current into the drain of M2, change included.
At the output node the two changes add: g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>id</sub>/2 from M2 and g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>id</sub>/2 from the mirror, giving g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>id</sub>.
That current flows into r<sub>on</sub> ‖ r<sub>op</sub> and becomes the output voltage.

blocks.text: Notice what the mirror bought you. The input difference produced a current g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>id</sub>, and all of it arrives at one node, so the output is single-ended with no loss of the other half. No separate differential-to-single-ended stage is needed.

sections.h3: Gain, output resistance and the price

blocks.text: The resistance at the output node is r<sub>on</sub> of M2 in parallel with r<sub>op</sub> of M4. Both devices sit in saturation, so both are large and the parallel combination is close to half of the smaller one.
R<sub>out</sub> = r<sub>on</sub> ‖ r<sub>op</sub> = r<sub>on</sub>r<sub>op</sub>/(r<sub>on</sub> + r<sub>op</sub>),   A<sub>d</sub> = g<sub>m1</sub>R<sub>out</sub>
blocks.where: R<sub>out</sub> is the small-signal resistance at the single-ended output node in ohms; r<sub>on</sub> is the output resistance of the NMOS M2 and r<sub>op</sub> that of the PMOS M4, both in ohms; g<sub>m1</sub> is the transconductance of M1 in siemens; A<sub>d</sub> is the differential voltage gain in V/V.

blocks.text: The price is two extra devices and a high-impedance node. That node with its parallel capacitance forms a pole at low frequency, which is why such a stage needs compensation inside a feedback loop (see 5.7). It also cannot drive a load directly: with Rout = 33.3 kΩ, a 10 kΩ load in parallel cuts the gain by more than half. A second stage follows (see 5.5).

figure.caption: The tail current sets the bias, the NMOS pair turns the input difference into two opposite current changes, and the PMOS mirror adds them at a single drain. The node at M2's drain sees r<sub>on</sub> in parallel with r<sub>op</sub>, so the gain is g<sub>m1</sub> times that resistance — here 1 mS × 33.33 kΩ = 33.33 V/V.

spec.title: CMOS pair with active load
spec.aria: Block diagram: a tail current biases an NMOS pair, a PMOS mirror acts as the load, and the mirror converts the differential current into a single-ended high-gain output.

examples.question: A CMOS differential pair with a PMOS current-mirror active load has g<sub>m1</sub> = 1 mS, r<sub>on</sub> = 100 kΩ, r<sub>op</sub> = 50 kΩ, and a tail current of 200 µA. (a) Find the output resistance and the differential gain. (b) Compare with the same pair using a 10 kΩ resistor per side and a single-ended output.
steps: Bias: matched devices split the tail current equally, so I<sub>D1</sub> = I<sub>D2</sub> = 200 µA / 2 = 100 µA. The given g<sub>m1</sub> = 1 mS = 1 × 10<sup>-3</sup> A/V corresponds to this bias.
Output resistance: R<sub>out</sub> = r<sub>on</sub> ‖ r<sub>op</sub> = (100 kΩ × 50 kΩ) / (100 kΩ + 50 kΩ) = 5000 kΩ² / 150 kΩ = 33.33 kΩ.
Gain: A<sub>d</sub> = g<sub>m1</sub>R<sub>out</sub> = (1 × 10<sup>-3</sup> A/V) × (33.33 × 10<sup>3</sup> Ω) = 33.33 V/V.
Resistor load, single-ended: A<sub>d</sub> = g<sub>m1</sub>R<sub>D</sub>/2 = (1 × 10<sup>-3</sup> A/V) × (10 × 10<sup>3</sup> Ω) / 2 = 5 V/V.
Improvement: 33.33 / 5 = 6.67 times, that is 20 log<sub>10</sub>(6.67) = 16.5 dB more gain from the same bias current.
examples.answer: R<sub>out</sub> = 33.33 kΩ and A<sub>d</sub> = 33.33 V/V (30.46 dB), against 5 V/V for the 10 kΩ resistor load — 6.67 times more gain.

traps: Using g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>D</sub>/2 for an active-loaded stage. The mirror adds both halves of the current, so the active load gives g<sub>m1</sub>(r<sub>on</sub>‖r<sub>op</sub>) with no ½.

Thinking the mirror load halves the gain or wastes half the signal. It does the opposite: it converts the differential current into a single-ended output current of full value g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>id</sub>.

Forgetting the conversion. Before the mirror you have a differential current; after it you have one single-ended node, and that node's resistance is r<sub>on</sub> ‖ r<sub>op</sub>, not r<sub>on</sub> alone.
Treating r<sub>o</sub> as a constant. It falls as bias current rises (r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λI<sub>D</sub>)), so doubling the tail current does not double the gain.
Assuming the tail source is ideal. Its finite output resistance sets the common-mode gain, so a poor tail ruins CMRR even when the differential gain looks fine.

quiz.q: Name the five transistors of the CMOS active-loaded pair and give the role of each.
quiz.a: M1, M2: NMOS input pair driven by v<sub>id</sub>. M5: NMOS tail current source. M3: diode-connected PMOS sensing M1's current. M4: PMOS mirror device copying that current into the drain of M2.

quiz.q: Why does a current-source load raise the gain without eating output swing, when a resistor cannot?
quiz.a: Gain is g<sub>m1</sub> times the resistance at the output node, so a high small-signal resistance is what is wanted. A current source has a large r<sub>o</sub> but only a small DC voltage across it, while a resistor with the same resistance would drop I<sub>D</sub>R<sub>D</sub> volts and push the output node to a rail.

quiz.q: An active-loaded pair has g<sub>m1</sub> = 0.5 mS, r<sub>on</sub> = 200 kΩ, r<sub>op</sub> = 100 kΩ. Find R<sub>out</sub> and A<sub>d</sub>.
A tail current of 100 µA feeds a matched pair with g<sub>m1</sub> = 0.4 mS and r<sub>on</sub> = r<sub>op</sub> = 250 kΩ. Find the differential gain.
quiz.a: Each side carries 50 µA. R<sub>out</sub> = 250 kΩ ‖ 250 kΩ = 125 kΩ. A<sub>d</sub> = 0.4 mS × 125 kΩ = 50 V/V.

quiz.q: The two PMOS devices differ in W/L by about 2 %. With v<sub>id</sub> = 0, what happens at the output, and why?
quiz.a: The mirror copies M1's current into M2's drain with a 2 % error. At v<sub>id</sub> = 0 the two currents at the output node no longer cancel, so the difference flows into the large R<sub>out</sub> and appears as a DC systematic offset voltage. The same mismatch also raises common-mode gain and lowers CMRR.

quiz.q: With matched devices, why is the common-mode gain still small even though R<sub>out</sub> is huge?
quiz.a: A common-mode input raises both gate voltages together, so the tail node follows and V<sub>GS</sub> of M1 and M2 barely changes. Almost no differential current is generated, so the mirror has nothing extra to copy. Only the finite r<sub>o</sub> of the tail source lets a small current through; a cascoded tail raises that resistance and improves CMRR.

quiz.q: Where did the factor ½ of the resistor-loaded stage go?
quiz.a: It is still there in each branch, but the mirror delivers M1's half into the same node as M2's half, so the two add back to g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>id</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real design the bias current is chosen by a g<sub>m</sub>/I<sub>D</sub> methodology rather than by formulas for strong inversion, because modern short-channel devices sit between weak and strong inversion. Stacking a cascode on top of this pair gives a telescopic cascode, and folding the mirror gives a folded cascode, both with much larger R<sub>out</sub> and gain. Foundry kits supply mismatch models so offset is predicted statistically instead of by hand. Search next for the gm/ID design method, telescopic and folded-cascode OTAs, and FinFET analog design.
